question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the given idiom.
Good grief
option_4: An expression of surprise or frustration
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. An expression of surprise or frustration.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom/exclamation "Good grief" is used as an expression of surprise, dismay, frustration or exasperation, similar to saying "Oh my goodness!" or "Good heavens!" (आश्चर्य या निराशा व्यक्त करने के लिए प्रयुक्त एक विस्मयादिबोधक)
◦ Example: Good grief! I forgot my wallet at home again.

• It is used as an interjection at the start of a sentence, not as a description of an action or a systematic process.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To dig a hole (मुसीबत मोल लेना): To create a difficult situation for oneself, often used as "to dig a hole for oneself."

• Option 2: To be very systematic: Means to be organised and methodical — unrelated to the idiom "Good grief."

• Option 3: To try everything possible: Means to make every possible effort — also unrelated to the meaning of "Good grief."

NOTE

• Similar exclamatory idioms/interjections tested in SSC exams: "Good heavens!", "For goodness' sake!", "Oh my God!" and "Gracious me!" — all express surprise, shock or exasperation.

• Do not confuse exclamatory idioms (used as interjections) with action-based idioms (used as verbs within a sentence).

question:
Choose the word that is opposite in meaning to the given word.
Temerity
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Diffidence.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Temerity means excessive confidence or boldness; reckless daring shown without regard for consequences or danger. (उतावलापन/दुस्साहस)
◦ Example: He had the temerity to question the manager's decision in front of the whole office.

• Diffidence means shyness or a lack of self-confidence; hesitancy in asserting oneself, which is the direct opposite of reckless boldness. (संकोच/आत्मविश्वास की कमी)
◦ Example: Her diffidence kept her from speaking up in the meeting.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Audacity (साहस): Bold, daring confidence — a synonym of temerity, not its opposite.

• Option 3: Assurance (आश्वासन/आत्मविश्वास): Confidence or certainty — again close in meaning to temerity, not opposite to it.

• Option 4: Poison (विष): Unrelated in meaning; a distractor with no connection to boldness or confidence.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of temerity: audacity, effrontery, impudence, rashness, recklessness.

• Other synonyms of diffidence: timidity, shyness, hesitancy, self-doubt, reticence.

question:
Some parts of a few sentences have been jumbled up, and labelled A, B, C and D. Select the option that gives the correct sequence in which these parts can be rearranged to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
The Ramayana is one of the largest ancient
A. 24,000 verses divided into seven Khanda (parts)
B. the first and the seventh being later additions.
C. epics in world literature. It consists of nearly
D. It belongs to the genre of Itihasa, narratives of past events, interspersed with
teachings on the goals of human life.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. CABD.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rearranging the parts in the order C-A-B-D gives a coherent, grammatically correct passage:
◦ "The Ramayana is one of the largest ancient (C) epics in world literature. It consists of nearly (A) 24,000 verses divided into seven Khanda (parts) (B) the first and the seventh being later additions. (D) It belongs to the genre of Itihasa, narratives of past events, interspersed with teachings on the goals of human life."

• Sentence-rearrangement rule: identify which part completes the opening fragment first (here, "ancient" needs a noun — "epics" from part C), then trace the logical chain — number of verses (A) leads naturally into which Khandas were later additions (B), before a new sentence introduces the genre (D).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (DCBA) is incorrect because it starts with "It belongs to the genre..." (D) directly after the opening fragment, which does not grammatically complete "one of the largest ancient."

• Option 3 (BDCA) is incorrect because part B ("the first and the seventh being later additions") cannot logically follow the opening fragment — it refers back to the Khandas mentioned only in part A.

• Option 4 (ABDC) is incorrect because part A ("24,000 verses divided into seven Khanda") cannot directly follow "one of the largest ancient," since the opening fragment needs a noun like "epics" (part C) first.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always look for: (1) the part that grammatically completes the given opening/closing fragment, (2) pronouns/articles that refer back to a noun introduced earlier, and (3) logical/chronological connectors.

• Here, the definite article "the first and the seventh" in part B only makes sense after "seven Khanda" has been mentioned in part A — a key linking clue.

question:
Some parts of a few sentences have been jumbled up, and labelled A, B, C and D. Select the option that gives the correct sequence in which these parts can be rearranged to form a meaningful and grammatically correct sentence.
Mr. Summers spoke frequently
A. the one that had been constructed when the first people settled down to make a
village here
B. liked to upset even as much tradition as was represented by the black box. There
was a
C. to the villagers about making a new box, but no one
D. story that the present box had been made with some pieces of the box that had
preceded it
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. CBDA.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rearranging the parts in the order C-B-D-A gives a coherent, grammatically correct sentence:
◦ "Mr. Summers spoke frequently (C) to the villagers about making a new box, but no one (B) liked to upset even as much tradition as was represented by the black box. There was a (D) story that the present box had been made with some pieces of the box that had preceded it, (A) the one that had been constructed when the first people settled down to make a village here."

• Sentence-rearrangement rule: the opening fragment "Mr. Summers spoke frequently" needs an object/preposition to follow ("to the villagers..." from part C); "no one" (end of C) needs a verb ("liked" from part B); "There was a" (end of B) needs a noun ("story" from part D); and "the box that had preceded it" (end of D) is explained further by the relative clause in part A.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 (BDAC) is incorrect because part B ("liked to upset...") cannot directly follow "Mr. Summers spoke frequently" — the sentence needs to first state what he spoke about (part C).

• Option 2 (DACB) is incorrect because part D ("story that the present box...") cannot follow the opening fragment directly, and this order breaks the logical chain connecting "no one liked to upset" to "there was a story."

• Option 3 (ACDB) is incorrect because part A ("the one that had been constructed...") cannot immediately follow the opening fragment; it is a relative clause that must come at the very end, after part D.

NOTE

• When a jumbled sentence contains a relative clause beginning with "the one that...", it almost always modifies a noun introduced earlier in the sentence and must be placed immediately after that noun (here, "the box that had preceded it").

• Always check subject-verb linkage across fragment boundaries — a fragment ending in a subject or preposition must be followed by a fragment beginning with the corresponding verb or object.

question:
Parts of the following sentence are given as options. Identify the part that contains a grammatical error. If there is no error, select 'No error'.
Ashwatthama, Drona's / only son, has had developed / a fondness for lavish living.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. only son, has had developed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The error lies in the verb phrase "has had developed", which wrongly combines the Present Perfect auxiliary "has had" with the past participle "developed" — this creates a non-existent, doubly-marked perfect construction.

• Rule: The Present Perfect Tense takes only has/have + V3 (past participle) — never "has had + V3". The correct form here should simply be "has developed" (Present Perfect: Ashwatthama has developed a fondness for lavish living) or "had developed" (Past Perfect, if an earlier point in time is being referenced).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: No error is incorrect because there genuinely is a grammatical error in the sentence, located in option 3.

• Option 2: "a fondness for lavish living." is grammatically correct as a noun phrase functioning as the object of the verb.

• Option 4: "Ashwatthama, Drona's" is grammatically correct — it correctly introduces the subject with an appositive possessive construction, completed by "only son" in the next segment.

NOTE

• Common SSC error-spotting trap: double auxiliary constructions like "has had done", "had did", or "is being do" — always check that only one auxiliary-tense marker is used with the correct form of the main verb.

• Present Perfect = has/have + V3; Past Perfect = had + V3. Never mix "has had" with a past participle to form a single tense.

question:
Select the most appropriate 'one word' for the expression given below.
Place where bees are kept.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Apiary.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Apiary means a place where beehives are kept for the purpose of collecting honey; a bee farm. (मधुमक्खी पालन गृह)
◦ Example: The farmer set up an apiary at the edge of his orchard to help pollinate the fruit trees.

• The one-word substitution specifically asks for the place/location where bees are kept — this is "apiary," which refers to the whole facility, not the individual nest.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Hive: This refers to the actual structure/nest in which a colony of bees lives, not the overall place or farm where multiple hives are kept.

• Option 3: Net: Unrelated — a net is a mesh material used for catching or covering things.

• Option 4: Aviary: This means a place where birds are kept, not bees — a common confusable pair with "apiary."

NOTE

• Commonly confused "-ary" place-words in SSC one-word substitution: Apiary (bees), Aviary (birds), Aquarium (fish), Vivarium (reptiles/small animals), Granary (grain), Cemetery (graves).

• Remember: "Api-" relates to Latin "apis" meaning bee; "Avi-" relates to Latin "avis" meaning bird.

question:
Select the word that is closest in meaning (SYNONYM) to the word given below.
Frequent
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Intermittent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Frequent means occurring or recurring often, at close/repeated intervals over a period of time — e.g., "frequent showers" describes rain that keeps happening again and again through the day. (बार-बार होने वाला)
◦ Example: The city experiences frequent power cuts during the summer months.

• Intermittent means occurring repeatedly, coming and going, or happening again and again at intervals, e.g., "intermittent rain." Of the four options, it is the only one that shares this core sense of an event repeating over time, which is the closest available match to "frequent" among the given choices.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Broken: Describes something that is fractured, discontinuous, or damaged — it emphasises interruption of a single continuous thing, not repeated recurrence.

• Option 3: Ceasing: Means "stopping" or "coming to an end" — this is close to the opposite sense of something happening again and again.

• Option 4: Inconsistent: Means "not staying the same; erratic or contradictory" — describes lack of uniformity, not the idea of repeated occurrence.

NOTE

• Stronger, more standard synonyms of "frequent" (outside the options given here) include: recurrent, recurring, repeated, habitual, persistent, continual.

• Do not confuse "frequent" (adjective — happening often) with "frequent" (verb — to visit a place often), e.g., "He frequents that café every morning."

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
I dump the tray on the side and start ______ up the dishwasher.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. loading.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence describes a person emptying a tray and then beginning the next physical task in the kitchen — placing dirty dishes into the dishwasher. The verb that logically and grammatically fits this action is "loading" (to load up the dishwasher = to fill it with utensils/dishes).

• Rule — contextual fill-in-the-blank: The correct option must both make grammatical sense (fit after "start ______ up") and make logical sense with the rest of the sentence (a kitchen chore involving a dishwasher).

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "tantalizing" means tempting or teasing (usually with something desirable just out of reach) — it does not collocate with "up the dishwasher."

• Option 2: "upbringing" is a noun referring to the way a child is raised and cared for growing up — it cannot function as a verb here and makes no sense with "dishwasher."

• Option 3: "alienating" means causing someone to feel isolated or estranged — irrelevant to loading a dishwasher.

NOTE

• "Load up" is a common phrasal verb meaning to fill something (a vehicle, a machine, a dishwasher) completely with items.

• Watch for fill-in-the-blank options that are grammatically the right part of speech but semantically nonsensical in context — always test the option by re-reading the full sentence.

question:
Improve the underlined part of the sentence. Choose 'No improvement' as an answer if the sentence is grammatically correct.
The actors is to shoot the scene three times.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. had to shoot.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The original sentence has a subject-verb agreement error: "actors" is a plural subject, but it is followed by the singular auxiliary "is."

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement: A plural subject must take a plural verb form. Replacing "is to shoot" with "had to shoot" fixes the error because the auxiliary "had" does not change with number (it is used identically for both singular and plural subjects), and "had to + V1" correctly expresses a past necessity: "The actors had to shoot the scene three times."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No improvement" is incorrect because the original sentence does contain a subject-verb agreement error ("actors is").

• Option 2: "had to shooting" is incorrect because after the modal-like structure "had to," the verb must be in its base form (V1) — "shoot," not the gerund "shooting."

• Option 3: "has to shoot" is incorrect because "has" is a singular auxiliary and still does not agree with the plural subject "actors" (which would require "have to shoot" in the present tense).

NOTE

• "Had to + V1" is the standard structure for expressing an obligation or necessity that existed in the past, and it works for both singular and plural subjects alike.

• Common SSC agreement trap: always check whether the subject is singular or plural before selecting a verb form — auxiliaries like "is/has" (singular) versus "are/have" (plural) are frequently tested, while "had," "did," "would," "could," "should," "will," "can" remain the same for all subjects.

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.
TARDY
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. PROMPT.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Tardy means slow to act or arrive; late; delayed. (देर से होने वाला/विलंबित)
◦ Example: He was tardy for school three times this week.

• Prompt means done or acting without delay; quick and on time, which is the direct opposite of being late or slow. (समय का पाबंद/तुरंत)
◦ Example: She gave a prompt reply to the email.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: BELATED (विलंबित): Means coming or happening later than it should have — a synonym of tardy, not its opposite.

• Option 2: OVERDUE (अतिविलंबित): Means not paid, arrived, or done by the expected/required time — again a synonym, not an antonym.

• Option 3: DELINQUENT (दोषी/चूककर्ता): In this context, means failing to do something that is required on time (e.g., a delinquent payment) — also close in meaning to tardy.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of tardy: late, sluggish, dilatory, laggard.

• Other synonyms of prompt: punctual, timely, quick, immediate, swift.

question:
Choose the option that is the correct indirect form of the sentence.
"Who is it?" Vikram asked, his euphoria fading.
option_1: With a faded euphoria Vikram asked who is it.
option_2: As his euphoria faded, Vikram asks as to who was it.
option_3: With his euphoria faded, Vikram asked who it is.
option_4: With his euphoria fading, Vikram asked who it was.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. With his euphoria fading, Vikram asked who it was.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The direct question "Who is it?" is a Wh-question, and when converted into indirect (reported) speech, two changes are essential: (1) the word order changes from question order to statement (Subject + Verb) order, and (2) the tense backshifts because the reporting verb "asked" is in the past tense.

• Rule — Reporting a Wh-question: Direct: Wh-word + auxiliary + subject...? → Indirect: reporting verb + Wh-word + subject + verb... (no auxiliary inversion, no question mark). Here, "Who is it?" becomes "who it was" (is → was, and word order changes from "is it" to "it was").

• The accompanying participial phrase "his euphoria fading" describes an action happening simultaneously with the asking, so it is correctly retained in its original present-participle form as "With his euphoria fading."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it retains the direct-question word order "who is it" instead of the indirect statement order "who it was," and it also fails to backshift the tense.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it uses the present tense reporting verb "asks" instead of the required past tense "asked," and it also uses the wrong word order "who was it" instead of "who it was."

• Option 3 is incorrect because it fails to backshift the verb "is" to "was" inside the reported question ("who it is" should be "who it was"), even though it changes "fading" to "faded."

NOTE

• In reported Wh-questions, never use a question mark, and never invert the auxiliary and subject as in a direct question.

• Common backshift pairs to remember: is/am/are → was/were; do/does → did; will → would; can → could.

question:
Find the part of the given sentence that has an error in it. If there is no error, choose 'No error'.
Democrats are often more receptive and accommodating of foreign people and cultures.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. and accommodating of.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence pairs two adjectives, "receptive" and "accommodating," but supplies only one preposition, "of," for both. The correct preposition that follows "receptive" is "to," not "of" — so the shared single preposition "of" is grammatically wrong for "receptive," even though it is correct for "accommodating."

• Rule — Parallel Construction with Prepositions: When two adjectives sharing a common object require different prepositions, each one must be given its own correct preposition; a single shared preposition can only be used if it is correct for both words. Here it should read: "...more receptive to and accommodating of foreign people and cultures."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "No error" is incorrect because a genuine preposition error exists in the sentence.

• Option 2: "Democrats are often more receptive" is grammatically correct in isolation; the error only becomes apparent when read together with the next segment.

• Option 3: "foreign people and cultures." is grammatically correct as the shared object of the two adjectives.

NOTE

• Common confusable prepositions in SSC error-spotting: "receptive to" (not "of"), "accommodating of" (correct as is), "different from" (not "than/to" in strict usage), "married to" (not "with").

• Whenever a sentence has two adjectives/verbs joined by "and" sharing one preposition or object, always check that the shared word works correctly with both parts.

question:
Choose the word that can substitute the given group of words.
One who goes on foot
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Pedestrian.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pedestrian (as a noun) means a person who is walking, especially in a town or city, rather than travelling in a vehicle; one who goes on foot. (पैदल चलने वाला व्यक्ति)
◦ Example: The pedestrian crossed the road carefully at the zebra crossing.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Hypochondriac (रोगभ्रम से ग्रस्त व्यक्ति): A person who is excessively worried about their health and constantly fears having a serious illness.

• Option 2: Vigilant (सतर्क): An adjective meaning keeping careful watch for possible danger or difficulties — not related to walking.

• Option 4: Cynic (निंदक/संशयवादी): A person who believes that people are motivated purely by self-interest and distrusts the sincerity of others.

NOTE

• "Pedestrian" also functions as an adjective meaning "dull, ordinary, unimaginative" (e.g., "a pedestrian writing style") — SSC sometimes tests this secondary meaning too.

• Other commonly tested one-word substitutions for people: Nomad (one who has no fixed home), Recluse (one who lives in seclusion), Misanthrope (one who hates mankind).

question:
Select the most appropriate antonym of the given word.
Sporadic
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Systematic.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sporadic means occurring at irregular intervals; scattered or isolated instances happening occasionally rather than continuously or in a regular pattern. (कभी-कभार होने वाला)
◦ Example: There were sporadic outbreaks of violence in the region.

• Systematic means done or acting according to a fixed plan or system; methodical and regular, which is the direct opposite of something occurring irregularly and occasionally. (व्यवस्थित/नियमित)
◦ Example: The scientist followed a systematic approach to testing her hypothesis.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Scattered (बिखरा हुआ): Means spread out irregularly over an area — close in meaning to sporadic, not its opposite.

• Option 2: Random (यादृच्छिक): Means happening without a definite pattern — again close in meaning to sporadic.

• Option 3: Rare (दुर्लभ): Means not occurring often — also similar in sense to sporadic (infrequent), not opposite to it.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of sporadic: occasional, intermittent, irregular, isolated, infrequent.

• Other synonyms of systematic: methodical, organised, orderly, regular, structured.

question:
Select the most appropriate one-word substitution for the given group of words.
An argument or statement seeming reasonable or probable
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Plausible.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Plausible means (of an argument or statement) seeming reasonable, probable, or believable at first sight. (प्रशंसनीय/विश्वसनीय प्रतीत होने वाला)
◦ Example: He gave a plausible excuse for being late to the meeting.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Incorrigible (असुधार्य): Describes a person or their bad habits that cannot be changed or reformed, e.g., "an incorrigible liar."

• Option 2: Corrigible (सुधार्य): The opposite of incorrigible — capable of being corrected or reformed.

• Option 3: Congruent (सर्वांगसम/अनुरूप): Means in agreement or harmony; in geometry, it describes figures that are identical in shape and size — unrelated to "seeming reasonable."

NOTE

• Do not confuse "plausible" (seeming true/reasonable, but not necessarily actually true) with "credible" (believable and trustworthy) or "probable" (likely to be true based on evidence).

• Related one-word substitutions often tested together: Implausible (not seeming reasonable), Cogent (clear, logical, and convincing), Specious (seeming right but actually wrong).

question: Choose the correctly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. MINARET.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The correct spelling is "MINARET" — a tall, slender tower, typically part of a mosque, from which a muezzin calls Muslims to prayer. (मीनार)
◦ Example: The minaret of the old mosque could be seen from across the city.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "PERTIMENT" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "PERTINENT" (relevant to a particular matter).

• Option 3: "OCCURED" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "OCCURRED" — the final consonant "r" is doubled before adding "-ed" because the stress falls on the last syllable of "occur."

• Option 4: "RELEVENT" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "RELEVANT" — note the ending is "-ant," not "-ent."

NOTE

• Doubling rule: when a word ends in a single stressed vowel + consonant (like "occur," "prefer," "refer"), the final consonant is doubled before adding a suffix beginning with a vowel: occur → occurred, prefer → preferred, refer → referred.

• Commonly confused "-ant/-ent" endings tested in SSC spelling questions: relevant, pertinent, persistent, consistent, dependent, existent.

question: Choose the incorrectly spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. CONSCENT.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "CONSCENT" is incorrectly spelt; the correct spelling is "CONSENT" — agreement or permission for something to happen. (सहमति)
◦ Example: The doctor could not proceed without the patient's consent.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "SPLENDID" is correctly spelt — meaning very impressive or magnificent.

• Option 2: "MEAGRE" is correctly spelt — meaning small in quantity or lacking in richness.

• Option 3: "MARRIAGEABLE" is correctly spelt — meaning of an age suitable for marriage. Note the retained "e" before the suffix "-able" (to preserve the soft "g" sound), unlike some other "-able" words.

NOTE

• "Consent" is often wrongly spelt as "conscent" or "concent" under the influence of words like "conscience" or "conscious" — remember consent has no "c" after the "n."

• Words ending in "-ge" usually retain the "e" before "-able"/"-ous" to keep the soft g/c sound: marriageable, manageable, courageous, noticeable.

question:
Select the correct passive form of the given sentence.
Ravish likes chocolate.
option_4: Chocolate is being liked by Ravish.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Chocolate is liked by Ravish.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "Ravish likes chocolate" is in the Simple Present Tense.

• Rule — Simple Present Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V1/V5(s/es) + Object
◦ Passive: Object + is/am/are + V3 + by + Subject

• Applying the rule: the object "chocolate" (uncountable/singular) becomes the subject, so the auxiliary is "is"; the verb "likes" becomes the past participle "liked"; and "Ravish" becomes the agent introduced by "by."
◦ Passive: Chocolate is liked by Ravish.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "was liked" is the passive form of the Simple Past Tense, not the Simple Present Tense used in the original sentence.

• Option 3 is incorrect because "were liked" uses a plural auxiliary, but "chocolate" is treated as a singular/uncountable subject, requiring "is," not "were."

• Option 4 is incorrect because "is being liked" is the passive form of the Present Continuous Tense ("Ravish is liking chocolate"), which changes the meaning and tense of the original sentence.

NOTE

• Verbs like "like, love, hate, know, believe, want" are stative verbs and are rarely used in continuous tenses in either active or passive voice — watch for "is being liked" as a common wrong-tense trap in passive voice questions.

• Always match both the tense and the number (singular/plural) of the auxiliary verb to the new subject in passive voice conversion.

question:
In the following question, out of the given four alternatives, select the alternative which best expresses the meaning of the Idiom/Phrase.
To jump out of one's skin
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. To be extremely surprised.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "To jump out of one's skin" means to be extremely startled, shocked or surprised by something sudden and unexpected. (बुरी तरह चौंक जाना)
◦ Example: She jumped out of her skin when the fireworks suddenly went off right outside her window.

• The image evokes a physical reaction so violent and involuntary that it feels as if a person could literally leap out of their own skin from shock.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To argue with someone: Unrelated meaning; there is no sense of disagreement or debate in this idiom.

• Option 2: To feel immense pain: Incorrect; the idiom is about sudden surprise/shock, not physical pain.

• Option 3: To show one's real side: Incorrect; this describes revealing one's true nature, which is not what the idiom conveys.

NOTE

• Other idioms of surprise/shock commonly tested in SSC: "To be taken aback", "To be thunderstruck", "To have one's heart in one's mouth" (to feel great fear/anxiety), and "To be at one's wit's end" (though this last one is about confusion, not surprise — a common confusable pair).

question:
Fill in the blank with an appropriate option.
Lecanemab was recently reported to have a small but ______ effect in reducing cognitive decline.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. significant.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "but" signals a contrast between the size of the effect and its importance — the sentence needs a word that means "small in size but important/notable in impact." "Significant" (meaningful, notable, important) creates exactly this contrast with "small."

• Rule — Contrast connector "but": When "small but ______" is used, the blank must supply a word that contrasts with "small" in a meaningful way (i.e., despite being small, the effect still matters), rather than a word that simply repeats or reinforces smallness.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "optional" means not compulsory, a matter of choice — it does not fit the context of describing the size or impact of a medical effect.

• Option 2: "marginal" means very small in degree or barely noticeable — this would be redundant when paired with "small," since both words mean roughly the same thing, giving no contrast.

• Option 3: "microscopic" means extremely small, almost invisible — again redundant with "small" rather than contrasting with it.

NOTE

• "Small but significant" is a common collocation in scientific/medical reporting, used to describe a modest-looking result that nonetheless has real, meaningful importance.

• Watch for "but" and "yet" as contrast signals in cloze/fill-in-the-blank questions — the correct option must create a genuine contrast with the other part of the sentence, not simply restate it.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

With his slight build and his simple white clothes, Narad (1) ________ harmless, but he had quite a (2) ________. He had powerful family connections and was a (3) ________ devotee of Lord Vishnu. His favourite (4) ________ was to travel from court to court and world to world, collecting gossip and (5) ________ mayhem.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. looked.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank is followed directly by the adjective "harmless" ("Narad (1) ______ harmless"), so the missing word must be a linking (copular) verb that connects the subject to an adjective describing its appearance, not a transitive verb that takes a direct object.

• Rule — Linking Verbs: Verbs like "look," "seem," "appear," "feel," "sound" are followed directly by an adjective to describe how something/someone appears (e.g., "He looked tired," "She seemed happy"). In contrast, "watch," "see," "observe" are transitive action verbs that require a direct object (a noun), not an adjective.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "watched" is incorrect because "watch" is a transitive verb requiring an object ("watched the show"), and it cannot be directly followed by an adjective like "harmless."

• Option 2: "saw" is incorrect for the same reason — "see" needs a direct object ("saw the tiger"), not an adjective complement.

• Option 4: "observed" is also a transitive verb requiring an object ("observed the ritual") and cannot correctly precede an adjective like "harmless" in this construction.

NOTE

• Common linking verbs tested in SSC cloze passages: look, seem, appear, feel, sound, taste, smell, become, remain, grow (when followed by an adjective).

• A quick test: if the blank is immediately followed by an adjective (not a noun), the missing verb is almost always a linking verb, not an action/transitive verb.

With his slight build and his simple white clothes, Narad (1) ________ harmless, but he had quite a (2) ________. He had powerful family connections and was a (3) ________ devotee of Lord Vishnu. His favourite (4) ________ was to travel from court to court and world to world, collecting gossip and (5) ________ mayhem.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. reputation.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence sets up a contrast with "but": Narad looked harmless, but he had quite a (2) ______. Given the rest of the passage describes him as having powerful connections and travelling around "collecting gossip and spreading mayhem," the word needed is "reputation" — meaning he was, in fact, well known (for being mischievous), despite his harmless appearance. The common expression "quite a reputation" fits perfectly here.

• Rule — Contextual cloze filling: The correct option must not only be grammatically valid after "quite a ______" but must also make logical sense with the surrounding sentences describing Narad's character and actions.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "disapproval" does not fit the idiomatic phrase "quite a disapproval," and it does not logically follow from the rest of the passage, which is about Narad's fame/notoriety, not others disapproving of him specifically.

• Option 3: "dismay" means a feeling of concern or distress — "quite a dismay" is not an idiomatic or natural collocation in English.

• Option 4: "censure" means strong criticism or disapproval — again, "quite a censure" is not a natural or idiomatic phrase in this context.

NOTE

• "To have quite a reputation" is a very common English collocation meaning "to be well known, often for a particular trait" (positive or negative).

• In cloze passages, always check that the chosen word forms a natural, commonly-used collocation with the words immediately surrounding the blank (here, "quite a ______").

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

With his slight build and his simple white clothes, Narad (1) ________ harmless, but he had quite a (2) ________. He had powerful family connections and was a (3) ________ devotee of Lord Vishnu. His favourite (4) ________ was to travel from court to court and world to world, collecting gossip and (5) ________ mayhem.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. formidable.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "He had powerful family connections and was a (3) ______ devotee of Lord Vishnu." Given that Narad is described as having "powerful family connections," the word describing his devotion should logically continue this sense of strength and influence — "formidable" means inspiring fear, respect, or awe because of great strength, size, or capability, fitting a devotee whose devotion (and connections) command respect. (दुर्जेय/प्रभावशाली)

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "brooding" means deeply thoughtful or anxious, often in a troubled way — this does not fit the description of a confident, well-connected devotee.

• Option 2: "pleasant" means agreeable or pleasing — it does not connect logically with the idea of "powerful family connections" preceding it.

• Option 3: "peasant" is a noun meaning a poor farmer/agricultural worker, which is grammatically odd here (it would need "a" not fit as an adjective before "devotee") and contextually contradicts "powerful family connections."

NOTE

• "Formidable" is frequently tested in SSC vocabulary and cloze questions; it can describe a person, an opponent, a task, or a reputation that commands respect or is difficult to deal with.

• Do not confuse "formidable" (inspiring awe/respect due to strength) with "terrible" (very bad) — though both relate to something impressive/intense, "formidable" carries a more neutral-to-positive connotation of strength.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

With his slight build and his simple white clothes, Narad (1) ________ harmless, but he had quite a (2) ________. He had powerful family connections and was a (3) ________ devotee of Lord Vishnu. His favourite (4) ________ was to travel from court to court and world to world, collecting gossip and (5) ________ mayhem.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. activity.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "His favourite (4) ______ was to travel from court to court and world to world, collecting gossip and spreading mayhem." The phrase "favourite activity" is the natural, idiomatic collocation used to describe someone's preferred pastime or pursuit — here, travelling and gossip-collecting is described as Narad's favourite thing to do.

• Rule — Collocation in cloze passages: English has fixed word-pairings; "favourite" most naturally collocates with "activity" (favourite activity/hobby/pastime), whereas the other options, though related in meaning, do not pair naturally with "favourite" in this sense.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "action" usually refers to a specific act or deed, or dramatic events (as in a movie) — "favourite action" is not an idiomatic way to describe a habitual pastime.

• Option 3: "bustle" means busy, noisy activity or excitement — "favourite bustle" is not a standard or natural English collocation.

• Option 4: "movement" refers to an act of moving, or a group working toward a shared goal — "favourite movement" does not fit the sense of a personal pastime being described here.

NOTE

• Common "favourite + noun" collocations tested in SSC cloze passages: favourite activity, favourite pastime, favourite hobby, favourite subject.

• Collocation-based cloze questions cannot be solved by grammar rules alone — they require familiarity with which words are conventionally paired together in natural English usage.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

With his slight build and his simple white clothes, Narad (1) ________ harmless, but he had quite a (2) ________. He had powerful family connections and was a (3) ________ devotee of Lord Vishnu. His favourite (4) ________ was to travel from court to court and world to world, collecting gossip and (5) ________ mayhem.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in the blank No. 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. spreading.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence reads: "...collecting gossip and (5) ______ mayhem." The verb "spreading" forms the standard, idiomatic collocation "to spread mayhem/chaos/rumours," meaning to cause disorder or gossip to reach and affect many people or places — matching the earlier description of Narad travelling "from court to court and world to world."

• Rule — Collocation in cloze passages: "Mayhem" is conventionally paired with the verb "spread" (spreading mayhem/chaos), just as "gossip" is conventionally paired with "collecting" (as already given in the same sentence) — both verbs describe Narad's habitual, wide-reaching activity.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "scattering" means throwing or dropping things in different random directions — it is used with physical objects (e.g., "scattering seeds"), not idiomatically with "mayhem."

• Option 3: "diffusing" means spreading out gradually in all directions, more typically used for gases, light, or tension being defused/reduced — "diffusing mayhem" is not a standard or natural collocation.

• Option 4: "advancing" means moving forward or making progress — it does not collocate with "mayhem" and does not fit the meaning of causing disorder in many places.

NOTE

• Common fixed collocations with "mayhem": "to spread/cause/create mayhem."

• Similar collocation pairs tested in SSC cloze passages: "spread rumours," "cause chaos," "wreak havoc," "sow discord" — all describing the act of causing widespread disorder or negative effects.
